name: BoolQ
description: A reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example consists of a question, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article, the title of the article, and an answer, which is either "yes" or "no".
creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
citeAs: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova. 2019. BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv:1905.10044v1.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was gathered using the pipeline from Natural Questions (NQ), with an additional filtering step to focus on yes/no questions. Questions were gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions were heuristically identified by selecting queries whose first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length. Questions were only kept if a Wikipedia page was returned as one of the first five results, after which the question and Wikipedia page were given to a human annotator. Annotators labeled question/article pairs in a three-step process: deciding if the question was good (comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information) before seeing the Wikipedia page; finding a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question or marking it not answerable; and marking whether the answer is yes or no. The final dataset combines 13k questions gathered from this pipeline with an additional 3k questions with yes/no answers from the NQ training set.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Manual Human Curator, Document analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and Wikipedia pages returned among the first five search results; additionally, 3k questions with yes/no answers from the Natural Questions training set.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Unlike in Natural Questions, only questions marked as having a yes/no answer were used, and each question was paired with the selected passage instead of the entire document. This was done to reduce ambiguity and keep the input small enough for existing entailment models. The dataset combines 13k newly gathered questions with 3k yes/no questions from the NQ training set, then splits them into a 9.4k train set, 3.2k dev set, and 3.2k test set, ensuring questions from NQ are always in the train set.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries likely to be yes/no questions were heuristically filtered using a manually constructed set of indicator words and a sufficient-length requirement. Questions were only retained if a Wikipedia page appeared in the first five search results. During annotation, questions could be filtered out if not judged good, or marked not answerable if the Wikipedia article did not contain the requested information. The final dataset only uses questions marked as having a yes/no answer and pairs each with the selected passage rather than the full document.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human annotators labeled question/article pairs in three steps. First, they judged whether the question was good, meaning comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information; this judgment was made before seeing the Wikipedia page. Second, for good questions, they found a passage within the document containing enough information to answer the question, or marked the question as not answerable if the article did not contain the requested information. Third, they marked whether the answer was yes or no. For annotation quality assessment, three authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples; disagreements were resolved by mutual agreement to create gold-standard labels.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: To assess annotation quality, three authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples and, when there was disagreement, conferred and selected a single answer by mutual agreement to create gold-standard labels. On these 110 examples, the answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels. Of the disagreements, six were ambiguous or debatable cases and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage. Because agreement was sufficiently high, the dataset uses singly annotated examples in the training, development, and test sets.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Three of the authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples for quality assessment.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Heuristic identification of likely yes/no questions using a manually constructed set of indicator words
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper states: "We present our data and code at https://goo.gl/boolq." No updating timeframe, maintainers, or deprecation policy are specified.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper argues that naturally occurring yes/no questions can be used to construct highly inferential reading comprehension datasets that have the added benefit of being directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions. It also notes that engineering datasets to be artificially difficult risks producing models without obvious end-use applications, whereas this dataset is tied to a clear end-task.
rai:dataBiases: Yes answers are slightly more common, with 62.31% in the train set. The paper also notes some correlation between question topic or type and the likelihood of a yes answer, and that some language patterns in passages may correlate with the answer. Questions are gathered only when a Wikipedia page appears among the first five Google search results, and the source questions come from Google search queries.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset uses singly annotated examples in the train/dev/test sets. Annotation can be expensive because annotators must search entire Wikipedia documents and read carefully. On the quality check set, some disagreements were ambiguous or debatable cases and some were annotator errors due to misunderstanding the passage. The dataset pairs questions with selected passages rather than full documents to reduce ambiguity, avoiding cases where a document supplies conflicting answers in different paragraphs. The paper also notes that the analysis of reasoning categories may be slightly out of date because the dataset was updated after that analysis.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as a reading comprehension benchmark for answering naturally occurring yes/no questions and for studying inferential abilities in natural language understanding. It is split into training, development, and test sets: 9.4k train, 3.2k dev, and 3.2k test. The paper uses it to train, fine-tune, and evaluate yes/no QA models.
